statement: A mineral is a naturally occurring geological material characterized using composition, crystal structure and physical properties under stated definitions.
Mineral identification uses multiple diagnostic properties because a single property such as color is often insufficient.
Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks are classified by texture, composition and formation history rather than chemistry alone.
The rock cycle links melting, crystallization, weathering, erosion, deposition, burial and metamorphism without requiring a single fixed sequence.
Geochemical interpretation tracks element distribution among Earth reservoirs and processes while reusing accepted chemical composition concepts rather than reteaching them.
Weathering can alter minerals and redistribute elements through physical disaggregation and chemical transformation in Earth context.
Earth is differentiated into compositionally distinct crust, mantle and core, with additional mechanical layers defined by rheological behavior.
Pressure, temperature and density generally increase with depth, but their profiles are inferred from models and observations rather than directly sampled through most of Earth.
Changes in seismic-wave velocity and propagation identify major internal discontinuities and constrain material state.
The liquid outer core and solid inner core interpretation is supported by seismic evidence together with pressure-temperature and material constraints.
Earth-interior models combine independent evidence and therefore carry uncertainty and model dependence.
Compositional layering and mechanical layering answer different questions and should not be treated as interchangeable classifications.
Geophysics uses physical observations to infer Earth structure and processes when direct access is limited.
P and S seismic waves differ in propagation and material response, providing complementary constraints on Earth structure.
Gravity anomalies reflect spatial mass-density variations but are non-unique without additional constraints.
Earth's magnetic field and magnetic anomalies provide evidence about core processes and magnetized crustal materials.
Geophysical inverse problems can admit multiple models consistent with observations, so uncertainty and independent evidence are essential.
B1.4-C03 applies transferable physics to Earth-specific inference without taking ownership of the generic physical laws themselves.
